title: Uber Redesigns M3DB Sharding with Subclusters to Limit Failure Impact
gist: Uber has repartitioned shard placement in M3DB, its distributed time series database, into fixed-size subclusters that each own a nonoverlapping slice of the shard space, so a node failure or maintenance event no longer touches up to two thirds of the cluster. The redesign buys bounded blast radius at the cost of rigid scaling increments.

themes.theme: Blast radius as the binding constraint

insights.claim: In M3DB's original placement model any node could own any shard subject only to isolation-group rules, so a single node failure could affect up to (n-1)/n of the cluster and a topology change could touch O(N) nodes.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Quantifies how permissive shard placement silently converts single-node faults into cluster-wide events - the same failure mode exists in many homegrown sharded stores.
insights.locator: Uber has redesigned shard placement in M3DB

insights.claim: Even with isolation groups mapped to three zones at replication factor three, a single M3DB node can share data with as much as 66.67% of the cluster, which increases recovery activity and forces maintenance operations to be serialized.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Serialized maintenance is the hidden operating cost of large clusters: it caps how fast a fleet can be patched or upgraded.
insights.locator: With the original model, any node could own a shard

insights.claim: Partitioning nodes into fixed-size subclusters that each own a distinct, nonoverlapping portion of the shard space bounds the impact of any node event; in Uber's example a 12-node cluster at replication factor three with six nodes per subcluster forms two subclusters each owning half the shards.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A reusable containment pattern for any replicated store where placement freedom has become an availability liability.
insights.locator: The new model partitions nodes into fixed-size subclusters

insights.claim: Uber scales by moving shards from existing subclusters into a new one using a greedy algorithm that simulates removing each candidate shard from the donor and picks the set that leaves remaining nodes most evenly loaded, avoiding a separate rebalancing pass and the duplicate network transfer and bootstrap work of moving shards twice.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Treating data movement rather than CPU as the scarce resource is the governing principle for cost of scaling stateful systems.
insights.locator: Scaling requires moving shards from existing subclusters

insights.claim: The placement algorithm costs O(S log S) for sorting plus O(S x N) for simulation, where S is candidate shards and N is nodes in the subcluster, keeping rebalancing decisions cheap enough to run inline with scaling.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Low algorithmic cost means the containment pattern is adoptable without a control-plane rewrite.
insights.locator: The algorithm uses O(S log S) sorting

insights.claim: Because destination nodes must stream data from existing peers before taking ownership of a shard, every unnecessary shard movement is a direct operational cost rather than a neutral bookkeeping change.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Explains why placement algorithms, not hardware, dominate the pain of scaling distributed databases.

insights.claim: The subcluster approach requires equal instance weights, scaling in multiples of the subcluster size, and a subcluster size that is a multiple of the replication factor, and it does not support changing the replica factor through AddReplica.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Rigid scaling increments mean capacity is added in large steps - a real cost model change for anyone running this pattern.

insights.claim: During scaling, cross-subcluster shard sharing can occur temporarily and only one partial subcluster is permitted at a time, so the isolation guarantee is weaker precisely during the riskiest operation.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Containment designs often leak during transitions - worth probing in any vendor's availability claims.

insights.claim: Uber kept M3DB's existing instance-level placement operations instead of introducing atomic subcluster operations, preserving compatibility with existing tooling and avoiding a large bootstrap in which many shards migrate simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Incremental migration over clean-slate redesign is what makes infrastructure changes actually ship at scale.
insights.locator: Uber retained M3DB's existing instance-level placement
